subject: A Proactive System of Intelligence for Security
body:
# A Proactive System of Intelligence for Security

Tomasz Tunguz

Venture Capitalist at [Theory Ventures](https://6a50e11d.click.kit-mail3.com/n4ulq8lp29svhx0r760u6h6439z7otlh7kerq/9qhzhnhdrqdo43t9/aHR0cHM6Ly90aGVvcnkudmVudHVyZXM=)

At the heart of every security team, there’s a database. That database records each time a user logs in, every packet of inbound traffic, & each attempted attack. Architected before AI, these SIEM systems are wooden shields in an era of autonomous attackers.

The consequences are mounting. Deepfake scams have stolen tens of millions. AI-generated phishing bypasses legacy filters. As [Mythos](https://6a50e11d.click.kit-mail3.com/n4ulq8lp29svhx0r760u6h6439z7otlh7kerq/e0hph7h7op78mos8/aHR0cHM6Ly90b210dW5ndXouY29tL215dGhvcy1nbGFzc3dpbmcv) has shown, the sophistication of attacks will only increase.

[Shachar Hirshberg](https://6a50e11d.click.kit-mail3.com/n4ulq8lp29svhx0r760u6h6439z7otlh7kerq/owhkhqhwdkw2xmtv/aHR0cHM6Ly93d3cubGlua2VkaW4uY29tL2luL3NoYWNoYXItaGlyc2hiZXJnLw==) & [Dan Shiebler](https://6a50e11d.click.kit-mail3.com/n4ulq8lp29svhx0r760u6h6439z7otlh7kerq/x0hph6he0re5k4b5/aHR0cHM6Ly93d3cubGlua2VkaW4uY29tL2luL2Rhbi1zaGllYmxlci0xMDIxOWI0Mi8=) saw this opportunity. Shachar led the Amazon GuardDuty product, scaling the business to over 80,000 customers. Dan built & led the 60-person AI/ML team at Abnormal Security. Together, they started [Artemis](https://6a50e11d.click.kit-mail3.com/n4ulq8lp29svhx0r760u6h6439z7otlh7kerq/kkhmh6hnvdnkz7fl/aHR0cHM6Ly9hcnRlbWlzc2VjdXJpdHkuY29tLw==) to build a database to power defenses for modern security teams. Within a few months, they have more than a dozen production enterprise deployments & are processing over a billion events per hour. We are excited to partner with them at the Series A, along with our friends at Felicis, Brightmind, & First Round.

[![Screenshot 2026-04-15 at 7.34.47 AM](https://res.cloudinary.com/dzawgnnlr/image/upload/w_1512,h_1006,c_fill,g_auto,q_auto,f_auto/kbwalimy5vuwszjff8yf)](https://6a50e11d.click.kit-mail3.com/n4ulq8lp29svhx0r760u6h6439z7otlh7kerq/25h2hoh3wv3k6vt3/aHR0cHM6Ly9yZXMuY2xvdWRpbmFyeS5jb20vZHphd2dubmxyL2ltYWdlL3VwbG9hZC9xX2F1dG8sZl9hdXRvL2tid2FsaW15NXZ1d3N6amZmOHlm)

At the core of this new SIEM are three technologies :

**Semantic understanding.** To a traditional SIEM, a log is just a string of text. It has no understanding that “jdoe” in Okta & “john.doe” in AWS are the same person, or that a sequence of individually benign actions might constitute an attack. Artemis turns raw logs into a living model of the customer’s environment : users, assets, relationships, & security posture.

**Agentic detection.** Legacy platforms rely on brittle, hand-written rules. An engineer writes a detection rule : “if events A, B, & C happen in sequence, fire an alert.” It works for a couple months. Then a new service gets added, log formats change, & the rule breaks. Artemis’ detections include multi-step reasoning agents that dynamically query data, perform aggregations, & reason about context to confirm a threat before ever surfacing an alert.

**Closed-loop learning.** Legacy platforms get worse over time : static detections degrade with changing data & behaviors. Artemis gets better : with each incident or proactive threat hunt, the system identifies new patterns. These are converted into permanent detections that are researched, validated, & maintained fully autonomously.

The result is a platform that doesn’t just store & search data, but *reasons* about it autonomously.

If you’re interested in learning more or joining this mission, check out the [open roles at Artemis](https://6a50e11d.click.kit-mail3.com/n4ulq8lp29svhx0r760u6h6439z7otlh7kerq/g3hnh5hmwdm4rnir/aHR0cHM6Ly9hcnRlbWlzc2VjdXJpdHkuY29tL2NhcmVlcnMv) & [Shachar’s post](https://6a50e11d.click.kit-mail3.com/n4ulq8lp29svhx0r760u6h6439z7otlh7kerq/n2hohvhv08vzmoa6/aHR0cHM6Ly93d3cubGlua2VkaW4uY29tL3Bvc3RzL3NoYWNoYXItaGlyc2hiZXJnX3NldmVuLW1vbnRocy1hZ28tZGFuLXNoaWVibGVyLWFuZC1pLXN

# Gaze at the Moon — Four Humans Are Heading to the Moon Right Now!

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!XRAR!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4565e472-8e66-43d7-8661-8ae71360a0fa_1280x720.jpeg)](https://substack.com/redirect/d4a58a39-44c3-476a-b9bc-18e558b30012?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

The view seen by the crew from the Orion spacecraft over the past few hours. Source: BBC

Artemis II, the first crewed mission of NASA’s Artemis program, successfully launched on April 1, 2026, at 6:35 p.m. Eastern Time from Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Over the course of this 10-day mission, four astronauts—Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch, and Jeremy Hansen—will fly around the Moon and return to Earth. Artemis 2 is scheduled to arrive at the Moon on **April 6, 2026**, during the sixth day of its planned 10-day mission.

This mission marks the first crewed flight to the Moon since 1972. The crew will pass within 6,000 km of the lunar surface and set a new record, reaching the farthest distance from Earth ever achieved by humans.

*At Space Ambition, it feels like we’re witnessing a historic milestone at the frontier of human knowledge and technology. It’s like watching a movie about the lunar program—except it’s happening in real time. To capture the scale of this moment, we’ve put together an overview of what’s happening with the Artemis II crew right now, what comes next, and why no one has flown to the Moon for the past 50 years.*

The primary goal of the mission is to test key flight technologies.

With the first crewed journey to the Moon in decades, many expected spectacular footage of astronauts landing on the surface. In reality, the mission is focused on something just as important: validating the systems that will make future landings possible:

* First, the Orion spacecraft will be tested in a crewed environment, including its life support systems, long-range navigation and communications, and the ability to perform manual control during docking operations.
* Second, the mission will validate the Space Launch System (SLS) in a real crewed scenario. The SLS—NASA’s most powerful rocket since the Saturn V—has already flown, but without astronauts on board. Artemis II is designed to confirm that the rocket is safe for human flight and that SLS and Orion function together as an integrated system. This is a critical step before any lunar landing mission.
* Finally, the mission will test the full flight profile to the Moon and back. This includes the translunar injection burn, a flyby of the Moon, and a high-speed return to Earth with atmospheric reentry and significant G-forces. In essence, this is a test of the entire mission architecture: navigation accuracy, propulsion performance, trajectory corrections, and thermal protection during reentry.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!imH5!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7923e218-b449-4bad-8268-aa667b5736d2_1024x627.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/652939e8-f2a2-4e1c-bdcd-329fa11ea50e?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

The launch of the Artemis 2. Source: NASA

# Problems From the Very Beginning

Despite the successful launch, the Artemis II mission did not go entirely smoothly from the very beginning.

*Importantly, these were not critical failures, but rather operational deviations—the kind that are expected during a mission of this complexity. This is especially true for the first crewed test of a new system.*

### In fact, the launch had already been delayed by about a month due to a hydrogen [leak](https://substack.com/redirect/3bc610e4-0890-4ea5-a09b-3ba291547119?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ).

subject: "Where’s all the f&$*#ing money going?" The Waste and Costs of American Utilities
body:
# "Where’s all the f&$*#ing money going?" The Waste and Costs of American Utilities

If there’s one obvious thing about this political moment, it’s that voters are furious about paying so much for electricity. In 2023, 70 million adults [chose](https://substack.com/redirect/13e83ba9-f3af-40af-8455-127641ebabf4?j=eyJ1IjoiZnZlciJ9.8N73-dqQlrWLx3o5gPfyirClhk7-cxP_NqOwOQYAApk) to forego food and medicine so they could afford their utility bills. Powerlines [found](https://substack.com/redirect/20ea0226-5c65-4cd0-8c72-29b0dbe98608?j=eyJ1IjoiZnZlciJ9.8N73-dqQlrWLx3o5gPfyirClhk7-cxP_NqOwOQYAApk) dozens of significant rate hikes last year, as the price of electricity [went](https://substack.com/redirect/4375b14a-6c3d-4ebd-ae12-00fef341c95e?j=eyJ1IjoiZnZlciJ9.8N73-dqQlrWLx3o5gPfyirClhk7-cxP_NqOwOQYAApk) up at one and a half times the rate of general inflation.

Voters have had enough, [telling](https://substack.com/redirect/c4042444-0f58-4e11-bca7-70deb4595e96?j=eyJ1IjoiZnZlciJ9.8N73-dqQlrWLx3o5gPfyirClhk7-cxP_NqOwOQYAApk) pollsters that electric utility prices are at crisis levels, and blaming excess profits for the problem.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!tgyD!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F735da5f0-a7db-457e-bfe7-6afa4ebe8b21_3193x1796.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/70cc4fa8-4433-42db-9dec-6c1bbc227d75?j=eyJ1IjoiZnZlciJ9.8N73-dqQlrWLx3o5gPfyirClhk7-cxP_NqOwOQYAApk)

And policymakers, such as Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, are [starting](https://substack.com/redirect/3c9af62d-1468-4da5-a52d-ecbc2a89a1c6?j=eyJ1IjoiZnZlciJ9.8N73-dqQlrWLx3o5gPfyirClhk7-cxP_NqOwOQYAApk) to talk about a revamp of the basic utility model.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!GAUb!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F89f54e62-0ec8-4f6a-90db-0c799ad5b8b9_718x309.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/a3f9e243-33a5-44e3-9889-71876384878b?j=eyJ1IjoiZnZlciJ9.8N73-dqQlrWLx3o5gPfyirClhk7-cxP_NqOwOQYAApk)

Investor-owned utilities, as well as some advocates for clean energy, disagree. They argue that the price hikes are necessary to address grid reliability, extreme weather, fuel price changes, the energy transition, old infrastructure, and so forth. The war in Iran is the latest argument for higher prices.

And there is some merit to that argument. Iran has raised costs, and someone has to pay them. But there is a problem with that argument as well. There are a variety of utility business models in America, and it turns out that publicly owned utilities are not raising prices nearly as quickly as investor-owned ones beholden to Wall Street. So something is going on with the specific Wall Street-driven business model.

Beyond that, there’s another more basic question. Investor-owned utilities, often consolidated into increasingly huge holding companies, have been hiking for years, which presumably should be bringing in a gusher of cash to fix the problems they observe with extreme weather and reliability. Yet we are constantly hearing that the U.S. doesn’t have a good electric grid, that we can’t keep up with demand, that China keeps expanding massively while we are stagnant.

If we’ve been paying so much more for so long, why do we still need more investment? Where’s all the f&$*#ing money going?

This discussion is now more important, because on Monday, NextEra, a Florida-based utility, [announced](https://substack.com/redirect/3b56b324-28b8-4680-b01b-b67b5ac95dd6?j=eyJ1IjoiZnZlciJ9.8N73-dqQlrWLx3o5gPfyirClhk7-cxP_NqOwOQYAApk) the largest ever acquisition in the utility space, a $67 billion takeover of Dominion Energy. The companies are claiming the deal will lower electricity costs and speed up the deployment of infrastructure for data centers using renewable energy. But the real rationale for the deal is entirely about how we price utility services

body:
# Smart tech is making war a dumber choice

[![The Economist](https://image.e.economist.com/lib/fe8d13727c650c7976/m/1/d2979654-fae4-451b-bdca-c79bb5522f6b.png;)](https://click.e.economist.com/u/?qs=ABB7InYiOjEsImQiOjQ4OTB9AAcAAAAAAfyUn7rFE9nmi3o3o2wRGTCoeiK6yxv_eZpIf4SUlVL7Ls4C_EbSCuA6urdgyfuN-FblfvQ4RUt7JKlnISfFNcEDaqbtEMQHbT2McT28urFb3Q)

May 28th 2026

![Highlights from the latest issue](https://image.e.economist.com/lib/fe8d13727c650c7976/m/1/1bd2eba9-7c72-4142-ba9c-3c1bffdeefe6.png)

Highlights from the latest issue

[![desktop](https://pas.economist.com/view/2/56924/9f13522fa690c061086a3872c30323fa/2190611?ad_region=Latin America&ad_country=Belize&send_date=28/05/2026&segment=4-BZ)](https://click.e.economist.com/u/?qs=ABB7InYiOjEsImQiOjQ4OTB9AAcAAAAAAfyUn7rGCduOGL9pfJKQu5daZjmTIu3I_yEQb0Ytf7jk0C3Jl1XDzGJk-z5rLoSgzA_8T9vHFsIAPfRWIeuS6x72XxtbRBDQ5Uub9tHKaAIH3w) [![](https://image.e.economist.com/lib/fe8d13727c650c7976/m/1/6fd080a2-d6e9-4dce-98f1-0f50c2ad84fb.png)](https://click.e.economist.com/?qs=ABB7InYiOjEsImQiOjQ4OTB9AAcAAAAAAfyUn7rIDn9WObAw4N-rUpi6QN-4-Xel9PITLSJz-uS-za-WR2T-mmBzy9RLmG00FosiVInSEeEcnTNp2amH-AsDvaMXfRK8zRCXk53R "") ![](https://image.e.economist.com/lib/fe8d13727c650c7976/m/1/8ae94367-2bde-424d-b6c2-36d6b9fe77f1.jpg)

Robert Guest

*Deputy editor*

One afternoon nearly 30 years ago, I stood on a hilltop watching a city burn. It was the day after South Africa had sent troops into its neighbour, Lesotho, to “restore order” after an army mutiny. It was supposed to be easy. South Africa is the big regional power. Lesotho is tiny. The distance from the border to the centre of Lesotho’s capital, Maseru, is only a few hundred metres. Yet somehow the South Africans messed it up, unleashing utter mayhem that ended with scores dead and mobs burning shops and factories to the ground.  

This forgotten calamity illustrates two truths about war. First, the leaders who order troops into battle are rarely as smart as they think they are. They overestimate their own strength; they fail to understand the other side. Second, when people see foreign forces marching into their country, they tend to respond ferociously. Both are reasons to be wary of starting wars of choice. This week’s cover story adds a third.  

[An essay](https://click.e.economist.com/?qs=ABB7InYiOjEsImQiOjQ4OTB9AAcAAAAAAfyUn7rJJVusLnlndV2qoJg9LZejGRxZ9ADXqnyYs1T7UjVFrl3CI9uZ7-6qt7trMEQbooznoABRaoTtQfm-ktIV6ucewEZ_zLUdyEes "An essay") by our outgoing defence editor, Shashank Joshi, describes how technology has made it cheaper and easier for weaker powers to resist stronger ones. Think of the swarms of Ukrainian drones that [obliterate Russian invaders](https://click.e.economist.com/?qs=ABB7InYiOjEsImQiOjQ4OTB9AAcAAAAAAfyUn7rKa-Zu8SDAP5npiK93xvn7LfdNA8PUB0P4Ga_PlI0dUBJ4l6FSJhcRDswM1EdtC0NQE6Qn-jYQz8bxKHzNXFjOP1_lMe26OLFt "obliterate Russian invaders") every time they try to advance. Or the low-cost Iranian munitions that have closed the Strait of Hormuz, hobbled the global economy and humiliated an American president. [In a leader](https://click.e.economist.com/?qs=ABB7InYiOjEsImQiOjQ4OTB9AAcAAAAAAfyUn7rLAkBRvUXESm4aI7nIyLajLvmkEbEArlTK7_yk19dFeAV9nN5vsoutHXuKWRa73meCifTPY6WSvEqX0zUCy9rJGID3PX5xCjMf "In a leader"),
 Shashank explains how these and other developments have changed the calculus of war. Attacking another country was always a gamble. As technology gets smarter, the odds for aggressors have got worse: wars of choice are more likely to end in ignominious failure. Xi Jinping might do well to read Shashank’s essay.  

This week’s edition of The Insider will dig deeper into all of this. Shashank will be joined by Adam Roberts, our foreign editor, and a panel of our correspondents. Subscribers can [watch the episode now](https://click.e.economist.com/?qs=ABB7InYiOjEsImQiOjQ4OTB9AAcAAAAAAfyUn7rMZH7f6deZeZBUCyV6itkEeKuy7Dh2zIAAIKpMNXMp2Dh8YLTD7anSwvUh9fbN4UMx2cmc_cZtgmBLHlkrzbYG41nMQtf9xOjo "watch the episode now").

body:
# Why Leaders Can't Delegate Judgment to Systems: Where Accountability Exists

#### About Our Contributing Expert

### Arun Gamidi | Enterprise Data & Analytics Leader

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!j0uD!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2121ff40-c33e-4780-8a61-9da11c672dd7_1600x900.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/bc18154f-059a-4ec5-b75e-b02cc5f66aed?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

[Arun Gamidi](https://substack.com/redirect/ccf65bb8-a299-4e47-b1c1-c268327f337b?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) believes most data initiatives fail not because of bad technology, but because they never connect to the decisions that actually matter. A data and analytics leader with deep experience in financial services, Arun has spent his career building and scaling data ecosystems in high-stakes enterprise environments where the cost of unclear decisions is real.

His work is grounded in a decision-first philosophy: data and AI create value only when they clarify the choices leaders must make. His framework, DATA by Design (Direction, Alignment, Trust, and Activation), gives organisations a repeatable path to align data initiatives with business goals, build trust in their information, and ensure insights reach the moment of decision.

Arun currently leads Enterprise Data & Analytics at MGIC. Through that work and his weekly Leadergence newsletter, his focus is on equipping data leaders to operate with confidence, not just access, in an AI-accelerated world. Readers can follow his ongoing thinking at [Leadergence](https://substack.com/redirect/206267df-d32c-4875-953e-7c1ce15741a5?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) on LinkedIn. We're thrilled to feature his insights on [Modern Data 101](https://substack.com/redirect/260901d8-43ad-411e-a3e1-d36405235f51?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)!

> *We actively collaborate with data experts to bring the best resources to a [20,000+ strong community](https://substack.com/redirect/8c3081f7-56c8-4c2c-9114-0839ae0cb77a?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) of data leaders and practitioners. If you have something to share, reach out!  
> 🫴🏻 Share your ideas and work: [community@moderndata101.com](https://substack.com/redirect/70bb27c0-ee52-4faf-9ca4-6bfc3922de2a?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)*

###### **\*Note: Opinions expressed in contributions are not our own and are only curated by us for broader access and discussion. All submissions are vetted for quality & relevance. We keep it information-first and do not support any promotions, paid or otherwise.**

---

### Let’s Dive In

Every decision has a consequence. And every consequence has an owner. But systems do not experience consequences. Neither can they own “consequences.”

They do not carry the weight of a wrong call or the satisfaction of a right one. That capacity belongs entirely to people. This is not a limitation of current technology, but a structural reality that more advanced systems will not change.

When something goes wrong, no one asks the model what it would do differently. They ask the leader responsible for the project or the model owner running the algorithm. That question has always pointed in the same direction, and it always will.

---

## The Problem: Accountability Drift

No leader decides one morning to stop being accountable. It happens gradually in the space between a recommendation arriving and a decision being made.

Systems are fast, and they are confident. They surface answers before the question has fully formed. That speed creates a pull, and most leaders do not notice they are following it.

The question shifts. It moves from “*What am I responsible for deciding?*” to “*What does the data say?*” That may look like diligence

# Linear #169.5: NuvoCargo, Their AI, & How To Sell Outcomes in the Age of AI Agents

---

When Deepak Chhugani started Nuvocargo in 2019, the startup HATED tech-enabled services. Then came the SaaS-only correction. Then the agent gold rush. Through every hype cycle, Deepak kept building toward one thesis: **customers pay for outcomes, not tooling.**

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!b3Q6!,w_1100,h_618,c_fill,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/l_play_button_usfui2,w_144,e_colorize:0/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-video.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fvideo_upload%2Fpost%2F191978774%2F3c370bc0-178c-40f1-8e66-1ac132253ac6%2Ftranscoded-00001.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/798dd34a-fe59-4202-b85d-39acf47b207f?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

In this deep-dive conversation on the Verticals podcast with host Nic Poulos, Deepak breaks down exactly how Nuvocargo went from a scrappy YC startup moving tequila across the Mexican border to an AI-native logistics platform with $85 million in funding, multiple acquisitions, and a product that’s making traditional freight brokers rethink everything.

Along the way, he delivers a masterclass in why most AI agent startups are failing to retain their customers — and what to do instead.

[Watch Full Episode](https://substack.com/redirect/7d079756-df62-424d-8bcc-1ba836b33f4c?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

[Listen To Episode](https://substack.com/redirect/a1de4789-1b80-4143-bba5-a726f56f3eb6?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!rRHa!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6826d5f2-8464-4cb5-9486-9066631ebaa8_1875x625.jpeg)](https://substack.com/redirect/775f3651-65c8-4643-8fa2-e8bf7595dbf5?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

Deepak Chhugani is the founder and CEO of Nuvocargo, an AI-native logistics platform powering North American freight. Born to Indian parents and raised in Ecuador, his multicultural upbringing gave him a rare edge in a market defined by cross-border complexity. He attended school in Latin America before coming to the US in 2010, where he launched his career on Wall Street at Bank of America Merrill Lynch.

In 2015, a twist of fate reshaped his trajectory. Deepak was one of thousands of immigrants who lost the H-1B visa lottery — “a third of folks in these high-paying jobs had to leave the country,” he recalls. Rather than let him go, BofA relocated him to their Mexico City office, where he spent years helping large family businesses and industrial companies raise capital, think about IPOs, and structure deals. That exposure to the Mexican industrial economy, combined with his family’s logistics business back in Ecuador, planted the seed for what would come next.

When he left banking, Deepak entered the startup world through a winding path — a mix of early-stage ventures and private equity, “1 to 2 years figuring out what the hell I’m doing,” as he puts it. He got into Y Combinator, went through pivots and idea changes, and landed on the concept that became Nuvocargo: a technology-driven logistics company focused on the massive, underserved US-Mexico trade corridor.

He was 26 when he founded the company in 2019. Seven years later, Nuvocargo has raised over $85 million from Tiger Global, QED, NFX, YC, and angels including the founders of Ramp, Nubank, and Deel. The company has made multiple acquisitions — in software, AI, freight brokerage, and customs — and expanded from US-Mexico cross-border to all of North America. Revenue is in the mid-tens of millions, and the company was recently named one of Fast Company’s most innovative startups.

# Import AI 441: My agents are working. Are yours?

Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe.

[Upgrade to paid](https://substack..EHnH4S5HHKtY7O9FyrSR-8tBDO7zZSZFkdbJQpsGTmc?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget&utm_content=185033372)

**Import A-Idea***An occasional essay series:***My agents are working. Are yours?**As I walked into the hills at dawn I knew that there was a synthetic mind working on my behalf. Multiple minds, in fact. Because before I’d started my hike I had sat in a coffee shop and set a bunch of research agents to work. And now while I hiked I knew that machines were reading literally thousands of research papers on my behalf and diligently compiling data, cross-referencing it, double-checking their work, and assembling analytic reports.

What an unsteady truce we have with the night, I thought, as I looked at stars and the dark and the extremely faint glow that told me the sun would arrive soon. And many miles away, the machines continued to work for me, while the earth turned and the heavens moved.

Later, feet aching and belly full of a foil-wrapped cheese sandwich, I got back to cell reception and accessed the reports. A breakdown of scores and trendlines for the arrival of machine intelligence. Charts on solar panel prices over time. Analysis of the forces that pushed for and against seatbelts being installed in cars. I stared at all this and knew that if I had done this myself it would’ve taken me perhaps a week of sustained work for each report.

I am well calibrated about how much work this is, because besides working at Anthropic my weekly “hobby” is reading and summarizing and analyzing research papers - exactly the kind of work that these agents had done for me. But they’d read more papers than I could read, and done a better job of holding them all in their head concurrently, and they had generated insights that I might have struggled with. And they had done it so, so quickly, never tiring. I imagined them like special operations ghosts who hadn’t had a job in a while, bouncing up and down on their disembodied feet in the ethereal world, waiting to get the API call and go out on a mission.

These agents that work for me are multiplying me significantly. And this is the dumbest they’ll ever be.

This palpable sense of potential work - of having a literal army of hyper-intelligent loyal colleagues at my command - gnaws at me. It’s common now for me to feel like I’m being lazy when I’m with my family. Not because I feel as though I should be working, but rather that I feel guilty that I haven’t tasked some AI system to do work for me while I play with Magna-Tiles with my toddler.

At my company, people are going through the same thing - figuring out how to scale themselves with this, to figure out how to manage a fleet of minds. And to do so before the next AI systems arrive, which will be more capable and more independent still. All of us watch the METR time horizon graph and see in it the same massive future that we saw years ago with the [AI & Compute graph](https://substack.com/redirect/cf6ea958-e570-4063-97ec-5e0465e49f9b?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ), or before that in the [ImageNet 2012 result](https://s

subject: Why Saudi Aramco Isn't a Proxy for SpaceX
body:
# Why Saudi Aramco Isn't a Proxy for SpaceX

Tomasz Tunguz

Venture Capitalist at [Theory Ventures](https://6a50e11d.click.convertkit-mail2.com/v8uxq0x97durhvlz85pighv0wngwmf9hkvrz0/dpheh0hevrolw9bm/aHR0cHM6Ly90aGVvcnkudmVudHVyZXM=)

After writing about the [SpaceX, OpenAI & Anthropic IPO liquidity problem](https://6a50e11d.click.convertkit-mail2.com/v8uxq0x97durhvlz85pighv0wngwmf9hkvrz0/z2hghnhen0kqrzfp/aHR0cHM6Ly93d3cudG9tdHVuZ3V6LmNvbS9zcGFjZXgtb3BlbmFpLWFudGhyb3BpYy1pcG8tMjAyNi8=), readers asked : what about Saudi Aramco? At $29.4b raised & a $1.7t market cap, it’s the largest IPO in history. Doesn’t it prove mega-IPOs can work?

Aramco isn’t a good proxy. The next biggest example, Alibaba at $231b, is a better parallel.

| Company | IPO Year | Market Cap at IPO | Market Cap Now | Float at IPO | Float Now |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Saudi Aramco | 2019 | $1.7t | $1.66t | 1.5% | 2.4% |
| Alibaba | 2014 | $231b | $365b | 15% | 86% |
| SoftBank Corp | 2018 | $70b | $66b | 33% | 60% |

In 2019, Aramco floated 1.5% of the company. Six years later, it’s still just 2.4%. The Saudi government holds 81% directly; the sovereign wealth fund holds another 16%. The IPO served strategic goals beyond capital markets.

Contrast Alibaba & SoftBank. Both started with real floats & expanded as founders & early investors exited. Alibaba’s float grew from 15% to 86%. SoftBank’s nearly doubled.

[![Alibaba & SoftBank Corp float percentage over time](https://res.cloudinary.com/dzawgnnlr/image/upload/w_1512,h_850,c_fill,g_auto,q_auto,f_auto/kcwxqcbwf7vqxiuy4k6q)](https://6a50e11d.click.convertkit-mail2.com/v8uxq0x97durhvlz85pighv0wngwmf9hkvrz0/p8heh9h4m82n5vbq/aHR0cHM6Ly9yZXMuY2xvdWRpbmFyeS5jb20vZHphd2dubmxyL2ltYWdlL3VwbG9hZC9xX2F1dG8sZl9hdXRvL2tjd3hxY2J3Zjd2cXhpdXk0azZx)

Float expansion is only half the story. The other half is timing. When do those shares actually hit the market? The typical IPO has a 180-day lockup, a period when insiders cannot sell shares.

[![Alibaba stock price with lockup expiration dates marked](https://res.cloudinary.com/dzawgnnlr/image/upload/w_1512,h_850,c_fill,g_auto,q_auto,f_auto/ctnnjx8r1sbzfowxfz9i)](https://6a50e11d.click.convertkit-mail2.com/v8uxq0x97durhvlz85pighv0wngwmf9hkvrz0/x0hph6heoxp5l8c5/aHR0cHM6Ly9yZXMuY2xvdWRpbmFyeS5jb20vZHphd2dubmxyL2ltYWdlL3VwbG9hZC9xX2F1dG8sZl9hdXRvL2N0bm5qeDhyMXNiemZvd3hmejlp)

The September 2015 unlock released 5x more shares than the IPO itself. The stock fell 52% from its $120 peak to $58, below the IPO price.

SpaceX, OpenAI & Anthropic may face less pressure. All three have run regular tender offers for years, allowing employees & early investors to sell before any IPO. SpaceX runs tenders 2-3x per year. OpenAI completed a $10.3b secondary sale in 2025. Anthropic launched its first tender in early 2025 at $350b. Much of the pent-up selling has already occurred.

But even Alibaba at $231b was a fifth to a tenth the size of SpaceX’s target. The market has never absorbed a trillion-dollar IPO where liquidity was the goal.

subject: The Most Expensive Dysfunction in B2B Product Companies
body:
# The Most Expensive Dysfunction in B2B Product Companies

Someone recently said something to me that I haven’t been able to shake. We were talking about a product team (a good one, by most measures) that had been heads-down building for months. They were shipping features, clearing the backlog, hitting their sprint goals. And yet the business wasn’t moving. Worse, the team didn’t realize that without that connection, the business would eventually stop scaling.

The phrase they used was:

> # **“We have to force the work back into connection with reality.”**

I love this phrase because of the word “force.” Not “nudge.” Not “align.” Force. It implies that the natural state of product work is *disconnected* from reality, that the drift happens on its own, and reconnecting requires deliberate, sometimes uncomfortable effort. And honestly? That tracks with everything I’ve seen over ~25 years of building software.

I’ve been writing about this problem, from different angles, for years now. So I want to use this post to pull those threads together into a single argument, because the phrase captures a pattern I keep coming back to: the gap between what product teams do and what the business needs is the single most expensive dysfunction in B2B product companies. If you’re new here, this is a crash course. If you’ve been around a while, it’s a reminder of why this stuff matters so much.

---

### What Disconnection Looks Like

Let’s start at the top. During my job search last year, I had a conversation with a CEO who described their last head of product as “the worst kind of nothing, an expensive nothing.” That phrase hit hard, and it wasn’t an isolated sentiment. I kept hearing variations of it across multiple CEO conversations: an impatience with how long it takes product leaders to create impact, a growing belief that the function hasn’t delivered ROI.

I wrote about this in [The Unimpactful PM](https://substack.com/redirect/66dc8cc3-6b95-4025-9b8b-512a30ff4c99?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ), and the pattern I kept seeing was structural: there are fundamentally 3 assets within a product company:

* product vision
* R&D resources
* the P&L statement

And you need to control at least one to have any shot at impact. Most product leaders who are deemed unimpactful never got the ability to pull any of these levers. The work was disconnected from reality not because the people were bad, but because the scaffolding for impact didn’t exist.

But even when the structural conditions are right, the drift still happens. It usually starts with teams losing their sense of direction.

---

### Why Teams Drift

I picked up a piece of trivia from a podcast a while back: the word “orientation” comes from The Orient (the East). In olden times, when a traveler was lost, they situated themselves by confirming they knew which way east was. To be “oriented” means to know where you are relative to your ultimate goal. I wrote a short post about this called [Disoriented Teams](https://substack.com/redirect/1bd39777-b216-4490-b9a2-dd171ff19b77?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ), and the core observation was this: as leaders, we spend enormous energy trying to make oriented teams more effective (better metrics reviews, tighter execution, faster cycles). But we underinvest in the lower-hanging fruit: getting *disoriented* teams re-oriented. A disoriented team isn’t just underperforming - it’s creating drag on the entire org.

So what keeps teams oriented? Strategy. But not just any strategy. A *coherent* one. After the Disoriented Teams post, a reader asked me: “are there systematic practices to prevent disoriented teams in the first place?” That question led to [Staying Synced on Strategy](https://substack.com/redirect/a6ff5efa-1ad2-4283-9f78-559467fd256c?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ), where I laid out 4 dimensions of strategic coherence:

* **legibility** -

subject: Considerations on Cultural Drift
body:
# Considerations on Cultural Drift

> *Like most humans ever, I love my culture. Its food, clothes, festivals, songs, stories, news, monuments, inspirational speeches, all of it. Deeply. They bring tears to my eyes, and comfort to my soul. I want to assume, as have most humans ever, that the mere fact that my culture exists suggests that it will probably do well by me. And the fact that it seems especially envied and celebrated raises my hopes further.*
>
> *[…]*
>
> *It turns out that, since I’ve learned about [cultural drift](https://substack.com/redirect/8f721b7b-7e79-498a-9480-947572f476f0?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ), I do in fact see my culture as broken. But for some reason I can’t or won’t look away. And I struggle to express to you just how very betrayed and adrift I feel as a result. I’ve lost my trust in something that I’ve implicitly and deeply loved and trusted. I will stay loyal to my loved ones, but I can’t stay loyal to my culture, including its key norms and status markers.*
>
> ~ Robin Hanson, [Betrayed by Culture](https://substack.com/redirect/78141d93-f4e2-4008-842e-f61b9fba1932?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

Robin Hanson is one of the few true polymaths of our age, his interests over the years including prediction markets, futarchy, human emulations, the importance of signalling to human psychology, grabby aliens, the sacred, and the fertility crisis. For as long as I’ve followed his work he’s been extremely optimistic about the future - from signing up for cryonics to pooh-poohing the risks from artificial intelligence, Hanson’s always seen the future as vast and bright - if not necessarily for biological humans then for our AI or emulated descendants.

But a few years ago, his writing took on a darker tone, and has been getting bleaker and more desperate ever since. He believes he’s identified a flaw in our civilization, a flaw that’s likely to prove fatal to it. [And virtually nobody’s listening](https://substack.com/redirect/14a5b199-96a9-4d11-aef1-a9d3f6cc2345?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ).

So I decided to investigate, by [interviewing Hanson](https://substack.com/redirect/4db38568-8cc8-4aa4-8419-a7ecff963252?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) and then by writing up my own thoughts on the topic after some hours of reading. If you want Hanson’s full views I recommend listening to the interview or reading the transcript; in the rest of this article I’ll summarize his argument and outline some of my remaining questions and confusions.

A core prerequisite for engaging with these ideas is the *Cultural Intelligence Hypothesis*, popularized in my intellectual circles by Joe Henrich’s book [The Secret of Our Success](https://substack.com/redirect/06598fe0-dbe8-4fb7-959f-b676e17c88df?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ). Henrich argues that the primary driver of humanity’ spectacular success vis-a-vis other species was not our individual intelligence, but rather our innate capacity for creating and maintaining *cultural* knowledge - i.e, copying the behavior of nearby humans, especially humans with high prestige.

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!C7ph!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fb40ea8d5-b579-420f-8b77-59ba89b389a7_600x406.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/af55fcd2-0908-4956-b0a1-1a6f0d14f821?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

Tomasello et al (2005) showing humans’ proficiency at cultural transmission

It is cultural evolution - the slow accumulation of adaptive behavioral patterns over millenia - that is responsible for modern civilization and everything we call “progress”. And, according to Hanson, this key driver of human progress [is now broken:](https://substack.com/redirect/42dd65a8-68e8-4805-

So if you're using Shield and looking for somewhere to land, here's the analytics recap in 2pr.io:

2/ Best posting times heatmap - by day-of-week and hour, based on your own engagement, not a generic chart

[Camila Barreto Lima](https://substack.com/redirect/2c85638b-c369-483d-9d2e-c0b8e87bde0c?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) is a Product Manager focused on building and scaling data products within **global digital ecosystems** across fintech and travel tech. She has led the end-to-end delivery of data products used in 55+ countries, delivering measurable outcomes such as increasing product adoption from 70% to 94%, enabling over $10B in transactions, and achieving NPS scores above 90%.

At *Conetic*, Camila **owns the strategy and delivery of data products**, defining roadmaps, governance frameworks, and lifecycle best practices. She works at the intersection of business and engineering, translating complex data and technical architectures into scalable, user-centric products that drive decision-making and operational value.

Previously, she has contributed to global platforms at *Dell Technologies* and other organizations, leading cross-functional teams across B2B and B2C environments. Her work consistently focuses on establishing single sources of truth, improving data accessibility, and embedding product thinking into data initiatives. We’re thrilled to feature her insights on [Modern Data 101](https://substack.com/redirect/ec0aa44f-c179-4fd2-a3b8-0fffec33a97c?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ).

Across industries, dashboards are built at scale. They sit on top of modern data lakes, cloud architectures, advanced models, and sophisticated BI tools. And yet, many of them fail because the intention is unclear.

**The roots of the failure are ultimately embedded in communication.**

[![The image shows a Stark mismatch between investments and intent when it comes to enterprise AI projects and initiatives as well as Business Intelligence | Modern Data 101](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!smXb!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fff4055eb-ee88-4de5-816b-e9bf700884e5_2360x1231.png "The image shows a Stark mismatch between investments and intent when it comes to enterprise AI projects and initiatives as well as Business Intelligence | Modern Data 101")](https://substack.com/redirect/dbb3b70c-c06d-4775-8342-06473d71dcac?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

# Nan Ransohoff: Finding Things Out, Double Life, Matriarch, Inputs, Evil, the Beatles

Welcome to a new issue of *Words That Matter*! Each week, we invite a guest curator to share the reading that matters most to them.

Nan Ransohoff ([@nanransohoff](https://substack.com/redirect/b6596dfa-e153-45db-a882-3dbc0552fee3?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)) leads Stripe Climate and founded [Frontier](https://substack.com/redirect/658ecedc-fe3c-4a50-a7dc-198adbfab934?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ), a $1B+ advance market commitment for permanent carbon removal. More broadly, her work focuses on incentive design to help solve important societal problems. Previously she built products at Uber, Nuro and Opower. She was named to the Bloomberg 50 in 2022 and the TIME100 Climate list in 2025.

Nan writes about topics like market shaping for public goods, moral imagination, and San Francisco culture on her [website](https://substack.com/redirect/761891d1-fb54-46e4-b555-d0c91f5d9e12?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) and [Substack](https://substack.com/redirect/d54ee593-88ef-4cf6-b64a-aa7ca4d85061?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ).

Please enjoy these works and words that have mattered to Nan!

## Nan’s Picks

### [The pleasure of finding things out](https://substack.com/redirect/f5b5af61-0ae4-4319-b8a6-1e96936b108d?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) (essay collection)

Richard Feynman

This is a collection of Feynman essays and interviews that are ostensibly about science, but really they’re about much of life – embracing uncertainty, finding the fun and mischief in things, dialing up wonder, exploring big ideas with both intellectual honesty and also a lightness. I forget how I stumbled across these essays originally, but for the past few years I’ve returned to them many times when I’m in need of a mindset ‘tune-up.’ They’ve become sort of medicinal for me – even ~15 minutes with one of them can reliably infuse my brain with a lot more color / texture / energy. (My favorites are:[The pleasure of finding things out](https://substack.com/redirect/c3cc129c-9b1d-405a-80d2-727eab9534dd?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ), [There’s plenty of room at the bottom](https://substack.com/redirect/4cad1588-2c2c-464a-9f84-b16b22341f89?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ), and What is and what should be the role of scientific culture? – but hop around at your leisure!)

---

### [The lives they loved – Regine Weiss Ransohoff](https://substack.com/redirect/bca7bc7c-fd90-4524-b3f8-405243eee78c?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) (essay)

Martha Ransohoff Adler

I’ll start with the obligatory admission that I am obviously biased here: this is a short piece written by my aunt about my grandmother when she died. Even so! I am pretty sure I’d still love this piece even if I didn’t know Regine. It’s a masterclass in capturing the essence of a person. You can feel how fierce, principled, irreverent, brilliant and witty she was, even in just a few short paragraphs. I think about this piece a lot. It makes me wonder what my (hypothetical) daughter would write about me. It forces an almost semi-regular check-in with myself to see if I’m living in a way that feels directionally aligned with who I hope and aspire to be.

---

### [The marriage question: George Eliot’s double life](https://substack.com/redirect/7f7eda3c-ebd1-4906-8a72-32e7ace9e269?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) (book)

Clare Carlisle

This book is responsible for my obsession with George Eliot (yes, yes, I too read Middlemarch and loved it, but this took the love to a new level). Among the many reasons to love Eliot is that she made some insanely bold/risky/controversial life choices by *today’s* standards, let alone for a

# Compacting...

[![Morpheus](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!VTm_!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa07322e5-1e94-4bf0-830f-cac23a76c79d_780x438.png "Morpheus")](https://substack.com/redirect/57174e64-b907-4bdb-a03d-a78cad62758a?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

There’s a difference between [knowing a path](https://substack.com/redirect/fa2aa787-da13-45f0-bfe3-4376399ac901?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) and [walking the path](https://substack.com/redirect/2289b692-5027-4eb8-9e96-9d57a06309ce?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ).

Here is how it happened:

Two days ago, Anthropic released [an enormous study](https://substack.com/redirect/fc6ba7de-aee1-4ac3-b82a-d709daa63a3f?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) on what people think about AI. Though the results of the study are interesting—people are both excited and nervous; they feel [its power and its burdens](https://substack.com/redirect/9211ea51-63f4-4027-a5db-689eb8567601?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ);¹ AI is [the light and the shade](https://substack.com/redirect/84b83610-e6b0-48e3-b2d6-5584c39de759?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)²—I was more immediately struck by the study’s methodology. In one week in December, Anthropic interviewed *80,508 people*.³ Interviews were conducted via a choose-your-own adventure chatbot. “Interview transcripts [were processed](https://substack.com/redirect/b650cd38-aa11-4a33-95d8-569639831a79?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) through a suite of hand-validated Claude-powered classifiers.” The groupings that Anthropic used to organize the responses were “designed first by analyzing answers with a [bottom-up clustering algorithm](https://substack.com/redirect/3879a5cb-e293-4c8b-bf74-50425bfac72c?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ),” and “categories were derived from clusters that surfaced during initial analysis.” And the final report was, no doubt, authored with the help of AI, and illustrated with graphics that were surely built using Claude Code. It was, Anthropic said, “the largest and most multilingual qualitative study ever conducted,” and it was done in three months.

An immediate story emerged: *This is the future we’ve been talking about*.

[From two years ago:](https://substack.com/redirect/d3267f4f-09c4-49dc-8bdb-da3c81cdb448?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

> If you had a day to save your [business], where would you go looking for answers? In your comprehensive database of financial indicators, operational KPIs, customer behaviors, and market trends, where every metric and insight is a query away? Or in 25 straight hours of unedited video interviews [with 750 customers]?
>
> Two things about this situation seem obvious. First, the actual solution to your [business’] problems is in the customer interviews…And second, despite that, you’d probably use the data, not the interviews. You have 24 hours! There are 25 hours of videos! You only have time to watch a few! You would be insane…if you proposed a bunch of changes based on a handful of randomly selected snippets of feedback. …
>
> [If AI revolutionizes how we work with data, it won’t come from analyzing numbers.] It’ll come from pointing AI at a new well—the unstructured video interviews in Dropbox—and letting us do the basic things with it that we’ve never been able to do before.

[From last year:](https://substack.com/redirect/23f3c629-5bb2-46e0-80b9-eee7582fcfb2?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

# Flying to the Moon and Mars: Engineering Challenges

**Issue 162. Subscribers: 84 439.**

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Nuqy!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa3920d00-4c77-4193-bb77-0994a6a56074_1280x714.jpeg)](https://substack.com/redirect/b97da528-2f76-4b25-aa4f-40a4c724996d?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

*Moon Base Alpha* by digital painter **Jon Hrubesch**. [Source](https://substack.com/redirect/2c03565f-bc23-4dfb-b3a6-18cd976f83e9?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

The world is watching the launch of the Artemis program — the US is returning to the Moon after half a century — and the space agenda is once again shifting rapidly. Even Elon Musk, long associated primarily with Mars plans, is now talking about the Moon as the next target. But behind the bold statements and the symbolism of this “return” lies a less visible, yet far more practical engineering reality: **on both Mars and the Moon, technology and crews will need to operate independently — making decisions, managing resources, and processing data without constant support from Earth.**

Once familiar technologies are taken beyond Earth, they cease to be “familiar.” **GPS is unavailable, communications are delayed or disrupted, electronics face radiation and extreme temperature swings, dust interferes with systems, and infrastructure is virtually nonexistent.**

In this article, we will explore the key engineering challenges of future lunar and Martian bases and examine how these solutions are already being tested on Earth — in environments as close as possible to those found on other planets.

While there are many challenges, today we will focus on three central ones: navigation, communication, and compute.

> We provide consultancy services for stakeholders in the SpaceTech and DeepTech sectors. Whether you’re an investor, corporation, aerospace agency, accelerator, incubator, ecosystem builder, startup founder, or planning to launch a SpaceTech or DeepTech business, we can help.
>
> Contact us at **denis@spaceambition.org**—we’d be happy to assist. Good luck with your future endeavors!
>
> *P.s. We have done a big research on space-data centers. Write to us if you want to receive it!*

## **How to Calculate Coordinates and Trajectories Without GPS**

The safety of the crew and the success of scientific operations depend on the quality of navigation on the Moon and Mars. **Navigation systems for off-Earth missions face several simultaneous challenges:**

* Determining the position of astronauts, rovers and equipment on the surface — at least within a local coordinate system linked to the base or landing module.
* Planning and recalculating the trajectories of lunar and Martian rovers, taking into account slopes, soil type, energy consumption, and scientific priorities.
* Testing the performance of navigation sensors and autonomous movement algorithms in the absence of GPS and continuous support from Earth.

On Earth, navigation relies on a global satellite infrastructure: GPS, GLONASS, Beidou, and their equivalents continuously transmit radio signals containing precise timing and orbital data. Receivers (including those in our phones) pick up signals from multiple satellites simultaneously and measure the time delay. By knowing the speed of radio waves, the system calculates the distance to each satellite and applies triangulation to determine its position in three-dimensional space, with an accuracy of meters and sometimes even centimeters.

# When Time Series Meet Transformers

[![](https://gallery.mailchimp.com/4c1d0cf4959586b47ef210e9c/images/ae24e896-3de7-4a4e-a678-06035fe33714.jpg)](https://quantopian.us5.list-manage.com/track/click?u=4c1d0cf4959586b47ef210e9c&id=1e3804e0d1&e=7d796f23db)

[Join Professor Esfan Haghverdi on March 3 for a live conversation with Marco Peixeiro, author of *Time Series Forecasting in Python*.](https://quantopian.us5.list-manage.com/track/click?u=4c1d0cf4959586b47ef210e9c&id=99789bf636&e=7d796f23db)

Hello Daniil,

If you’ve ever had a credit card, you’ve probably lived this moment: you’re buying dinner in a new city, or making a purchase that’s slightly higher than your usual spending, and your card is suddenly declined for suspected fraud. Annoying, yes. But from your bank’s point of view, that swipe is not just a single event. It is the latest point in a sequence. Banks analyze spending as a living timeline: how often you buy things, what you normally spend, when you spend, and what kinds of merchants you use. That timeline is a time series, and it is messy, irregular, and full of context.

Fraud detection is fundamentally about modeling behavior over time. The challenge is that transaction time series are not neat or evenly spaced, and “normal” behavior can shift depending on the person, the day, or the situation. A useful model needs to understand both short-term context and long-term patterns, then decide whether a new transaction is genuinely suspicious or simply unusual.

This is one reason Transformers have drawn so much attention in time series research. Attention-based models offer a flexible way to learn from sequential data, and researchers have explored many adaptations to make Transformers work better for time series challenges like long sequences, seasonality, and non-stationary patterns. “Transformers in Time Series: A Survey” by Wen et al. provides a structured overview of this research, organizing the field around both how Transformer architectures are modified and where they are applied across forecasting, anomaly detection, and classification.

You can find more details about the paper in the section below. And if you’d like to hear more about the practical applications of time series in finance, join [our next Quantopian book series conversation](https://quantopian.us5.list-manage.com/track/click?u=4c1d0cf4959586b47ef210e9c&id=24fd984985&e=7d796f23db) with Marco Peixeiro, author of *Time Series Forecasting in Python*.

### Paper Summary

The paper, “Transformers in Time Series: A Survey” by Qingsong Wen, Tian Zhou, Chaoli Zhang, Weiqi Chen, Ziqing Ma, Junchi Yan, and Liang Sun, reviews how Transformer models have been adapted for time series analysis, motivated by their ability to capture long-range dependencies. The authors organize prior work using a taxonomy from two perspectives: network modifications (positional/timestamp encoding, attention changes, and architecture-level redesigns) and application domains, especially forecasting, anomaly detection, and classification. They summarize representative models and discuss the main design trends that make Transformers better suited for time series data.

The paper also includes experiments to understand how Transformers behave on time series benchmarks, showing that many variants still struggle to benefit from very long input sequences. The authors find that increasing model depth does not consistently improve results, unlike in NLP and vision. A major takeaway is that injecting time-series inductive biases—particularly seasonal-trend decomposition—can strongly boost forecasting performance. The survey ends by highlighting future directions such as improved inductive biases, Transformer+GNN hybrids for spatio-temporal data, and pretraining for time series Transformers.

[![](https://mcusercontent.com/4c1d0cf4959586b47ef210e9c/images/fa8aa542-0560-ce8c-89e2-583a28d6e406.png)](https://quantopian.us5.list-manage.com/track/click?u=4c1d0cf4959586b47ef210e9c&id=7f7d

# 7 Minutes to Understand the New Spark Streaming Feature that Changes Everything

#### About Our Contributing Expert

### Vi Trinh | Data Engineer

**[Vu Trinh](https://substack.com/redirect/a4292f36-6470-49f1-b6ae-49837e4fe9a5?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)** is a Data Engineer and educator known for breaking down complex data engineering concepts into simple, structured explanations. Currently working at **Amanotes**, a music game company, Vu combines hands-on industry experience with a deep passion for learning and teaching.

He is the creator of **[VuTrinh](https://substack.com/redirect/8fb22d20-91cc-4843-a290-8f3cf316e9da?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)**, a fast-growing newsletter read by **[17,000+ data engineers](https://substack.com/redirect/8fb22d20-91cc-4843-a290-8f3cf316e9da?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)** worldwide. Through long-form articles and curated weekly resources, Vu explores everything from Apache Spark internals and lakehouse table formats to BigQuery pricing models and the evolution of data engineering itself. His writing is practical, research-driven, and grounded in first principles.

Based in Ho Chi Minh City, Vu’s mission is simple: cut through shallow content and help engineers truly understand how data systems work under the hood. As he often says, his mom started reading his articles to support her son, and now she can design data architectures and write ETL scripts! We’re thrilled to feature his unique insights on [Modern Data 101](https://substack.com/redirect/fc4717c9-e35c-44ad-8e4a-583bdadf8e64?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)!

> *We actively collaborate with data experts to bring the best resources to a [15,000+ strong community](https://substack.com/redirect/b98d957e-c8db-4d63-9703-4df9547dd589?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) of data leaders and practitioners. If you have something to share, reach out!  
> 🫴🏻 Share your ideas and work: [community@moderndata101.com](https://substack.com/redirect/91a32fe2-d2a6-4b37-be37-737ed4281c8d?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)*

###### **\*Note: Opinions expressed in contributions are not our own and are only curated by us for broader access and discussion. All submissions are vetted for quality & relevance. We keep it information-first and do not support any promotions, paid or otherwise.**

---

## Let’s Dive In

Apache Spark now cares about the ultra-low latency.

[![7 Minutes to Understand the New Spark Streaming Feature that Changes Everything | Modern Data 101](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!RmXA!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F9e6453f0-51bf-4e26-b165-d371aac02007_1456x1040.png "7 Minutes to Understand the New Spark Streaming Feature that Changes Everything | Modern Data 101")](https://substack.com/redirect/0d094c9b-b262-4d3a-85ed-fa278def4c92?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

When it comes to stream processing, everybody usually brings Spark and Flink to the table. Flink is famous for its true stream processing: every record is processed continuously, nearly as soon as it arrives. Spark Structured Streaming, on the other hand, relies on its batch-processing engine to process a continuous stream in microbatches.

The latency is indeed higher than Flink’s; however, Spark has the advantage of its user base: many users already use Spark, and if they want to switch from batch to stream processing, they only need to tweak the code a bit.

Thus, you commonly see advice like this: “Only if you actually need millisecond latency, invest in Flink. Spark is still a good choice for second-tier latency use cases, given its simplicity and familiarity (Flink has a steep learning curve and requires significant resources to man

## **Around the Horn (24th episode)**

That weekday 4PM central time slot beckons: let’s go back Around the Horn!

[![Around the Horn - Wikipedia](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Vckw!,w_358,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F634c73fc-853b-4e16-a7a4-d8a58c45cc2f_358x197.jpeg "Around the Horn - Wikipedia")](https://substack.com/redirect/218bc786-8f78-4220-b5fa-3fe312b11391?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

Welcome to episode 24. For new readers, here’s how it works (see **[ChinAI #342](https://substack.com/redirect/3fe66d71-5e53-4d1d-8cf8-65c2b66420a9?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)** for the previous edition):

* I give short previews of ten articles that caught my eye during a scan through my usual sources (all published within the past week or so). The title for each preview links to the original article in Chinese.
* Readers vote on next week’s feature translation by replying to the email and/or commenting on the post with the number of your preferred article. *\*As a show of appreciation to readers who support ChinAI through a paid subscription, I’ll give some added weight to those votes.*
* The main idea is that any of these 10 links would have made for a great feature translation this week — like season 4 of Industry, there are no skips!

#### **1) [China is stirring up an OpenClaw tempest](https://substack.com/redirect/56f03e36-6828-4588-a8c5-484f548eb521?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)**

**Summary:** Last week, I noted how OpenClaw enthusiasts factor into MiniMax’s popularity on OpenRouter. This article reports on OpenClaw’s China community, including Tencent and other big cloud providers setting up offline “booths” to help people deploy open-source agents.

**Source: All Weather TMT [全天候科技]** - article recommended by Huxiu platform

#### **2) [MiniMax hasn’t gone crazy, the market has gone crazy](https://substack.com/redirect/5d1f8088-c356-4c04-bc8a-ebc0e8e62796?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)**

**Summary:** By March 3rd, MiniMax ranked as the fifth largest technology stock on Hong Kong’s stock exchange, nearing Baidu and JD.com’s value. Is this real? What do the R&D efficiency numbers show? How will geopolitics and international regulations affect its rise?

**Source: 虎嗅 (**Huxiu) — well-known platform that shares user-generated content but also publishes their own pieces on China’s science and technology ecosystem.

subject: The AI Acqui-Hire Wave
body:
# The AI Acqui-Hire Wave

Tomasz Tunguz

Venture Capitalist at [Theory Ventures](https://6a50e11d.click.convertkit-mail2.com/r8uklqk5nptoh34w8krc2hdnn8n66s7hwl39x/9qhzhnhd0x57g7t9/aHR0cHM6Ly90aGVvcnkudmVudHVyZXM=)

Scale AI sold for $14.8 billion.[1](#fn:1) Character.AI for $2.5 billion.[2](#fn:2) Inflection for $650 million.[3](#fn:3) They represent a tiny fraction of the market.

[![AI Acqui-Hires by Year](https://res.cloudinary.com/dzawgnnlr/image/upload/w_1512,h_850,c_fill,g_auto,q_auto,f_auto/ueq2i4nmgon2o9hj7wtl)](https://6a50e11d.click.convertkit-mail2.com/r8uklqk5nptoh34w8krc2hdnn8n66s7hwl39x/owhkhqhwpnqzrxcv/aHR0cHM6Ly9yZXMuY2xvdWRpbmFyeS5jb20vZHphd2dubmxyL2ltYWdlL3VwbG9hZC9xX2F1dG8sZl9hdXRvL3VlcTJpNG5tZ29uMm85aGo3d3Rs)

From 2020 to 2025, there were 5,700 AI & ML acquisitions. Only 21% disclosed a deal value. The remaining 4,500 share a pattern : small teams absorbed into larger companies. No fanfare. No valuation headlines. Just talent migrating from startup to incumbent.

It’s cheaper to buy a team than to compete for hires or build from scratch.

[![Top AI Acquirers : Disclosed vs Undisclosed Deals](https://res.cloudinary.com/dzawgnnlr/image/upload/w_1512,h_1702,c_fill,g_auto,q_auto,f_auto/wdsgrw532ppkfdjrm7hl)](https://6a50e11d.click.convertkit-mail2.com/r8uklqk5nptoh34w8krc2hdnn8n66s7hwl39x/z2hghnhen7lg3nhp/aHR0cHM6Ly9yZXMuY2xvdWRpbmFyeS5jb20vZHphd2dubmxyL2ltYWdlL3VwbG9hZC9xX2F1dG8sZl9hdXRvL3dkc2dydzUzMnBwa2ZkanJtN2hs)

The buyers are surprising. Accenture leads with 21 AI acquisitions, only three disclosed. Apple follows with 17, just two disclosed. Google & Microsoft rank far lower.

[![AI Acquisition Deal Size Distribution](https://res.cloudinary.com/dzawgnnlr/image/upload/w_1512,h_850,c_fill,g_auto,q_auto,f_auto/qcybd6fc9esqpemdsmok)](https://6a50e11d.click.convertkit-mail2.com/r8uklqk5nptoh34w8krc2hdnn8n66s7hwl39x/e0hph7h76erx03f8/aHR0cHM6Ly9yZXMuY2xvdWRpbmFyeS5jb20vZHphd2dubmxyL2ltYWdlL3VwbG9hZC9xX2F1dG8sZl9hdXRvL3FjeWJkNmZjOWVzcXBlbWRzbW9r)

The 75th percentile deal size tripled from $82M in 2020 to $248M in 2025. The urgency behind developing a strong AI strategy is rising.

The undisclosed majority likely falls well below these figures. 398 undisclosed AI deals in 2020 grew to 1,271 by 2025. Four thousand AI teams absorbed in five years. The pace is quickening.[4](#fn:4)

---

---

1. Meta acquired a 49% stake in Scale AI for $14.8 billion in June 2025. [↩︎](#fnref:1)
2. Google paid $2.5 billion for a non-exclusive license and Character.AI’s founders. [↩︎](#fnref:2)
3. Microsoft paid $650 million for Inflection’s talent, including Mustafa Suleyman. [↩︎](#fnref:3)
4. Thank you to PitchBook for helping pull this data together. [↩︎](#fnref:4)

subject: How I built a new composite qualitative metric - The Lovable Score
body:
# How I built a new composite qualitative metric - The Lovable Score

Growth teams love metrics they can screenshot in a dashboard.

Usage.  
Conversion.  
Retention.  
Revenue.

A much less comfortable question: do users actually give a shit?

Because a lot of “healthy” products are really just products people tolerate:  
their boss told them to use it, they have not found a better alternative yet, or switching feels too annoying.

None of that means they love it.

And the second a real alternative shows up, they’re gone. There goes your retention.

If you want durable growth, the distinction between “I have to use it” and “I love using it” matters a lot.

---

*Hey, quick heads-up! I’m going to be doing something new with my sponsors - specifically focusing on sharing products that I use myself or personally recommend to others. More on this soon, but this week I’m excited to share about one of my faves: **Passionfroot.***

***Passionfroot helps b2b marketing/growth teams work with creators** ([like me](https://substack.com/redirect/73646880-6f3f-4318-9085-bbbe5a27e3b6?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)!) And they just released their new AI agent, **Zest**, which can run your entire creator-led GTM from just a prompt. You get:*

* *A full campaign strategy (based on your ICP, channels, content format preferences & budget)*
* *Suggested channel mix (across LinkedIn, YouTube, X, Insta, TikTok)*
* *A list of the specific creators you should work with (even if they’re not on Passionfroot)*
* *Personalized outreach drafts*
* *Full campaign management & reporting*

*They really do it all for you. If you’re planning a big launch, announcement, or other campaign and want to amplify it with creator partnerships - I’d definitely recommend trying Passionfroot and Zest. **Learn more, [here](https://substack.com/redirect/e5093106-65b5-433f-b5d0-897354e5ead8?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ).***

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!0v5Q!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd0301f98-ffaa-44fb-9f23-436d04c957b3_1600x400.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/826e139c-cfb0-442f-93de-ceed13cbd779?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

---

As I’ve been talking more and more about the importance of customer trust and emotional connection in product development/growth (see: [Brand is a product job now](https://substack.com/redirect/dc037245-5e62-4410-9782-8b25819e6e68?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) and [Minimum Lovable Product era](https://substack.com/redirect/db68a00d-98a2-40dd-a05c-b0bcc8653ce4?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)), I can just see the looks of unease/disgust on the faces of my super quantitative peers. ‘You want us to optimize for… feelings?’

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!xfqb!,w_396,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fca4358b7-6abb-4d0f-911f-11643615beb5_500x582.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/a5adbd42-eef4-4bfe-855f-56f0ed7ecad8?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

I see it all over: Most really strong Growth orgs struggle with integrating qualitative insights. The same thing that makes a team elite at rigorously tracking, analyzing, and applying quantitative data can make them avoid the squishier parts of non-numerical inputs. In today’s tech landscape, feature differentiation is collapsing. Growth is becoming a [trust problem](https://substack.com/redirect/897d72bd-6b5c-476e-be27-1d517f3a7231?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ), and the products making the biggest splash are the ones [people genuinely love](https://substack.com/redirect/db68a00d-98a2-40dd-a05c-b0bcc8653ce4?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvo

# [AINews] The Two Sides of OpenClaw

In an opportune coinciding of big three letter conferences, the [TED talk](https://substack.com/redirect/140de1de-9d8c-4a2d-8e64-e8f8395d1ff5?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) and the [AIE talks](https://substack.com/redirect/940cfdb8-2623-415a-9349-90fb95558858?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ) of Peter Steinberger dropped today. To the general public, the inspiring story of OpenClaw was delightfully [told onstage](https://substack.com/redirect/48752db4-dbc5-4594-9468-13a3fae33a5c?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ), which recaps all the highs:

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!w4xU!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd938eb29-488f-4a91-9b9d-7ba5dabf55af_1416x1022.png)](https://substack.com/redirect/8ad8b935-5f8d-4814-90f6-6137a2f95bfb?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

To the engineering audience, it was more sober, talking about the unprecedented levels of security incidents (60x more reports than curl, at least 20% of skill contributions malicious) and scaling issues involved in maintaining the fastest growing open source project in history:

[![](https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/zgNvts_2TUE)](https://substack.com/redirect/a48b0aa2-e92d-4e88-979f-a06ac20ab0bb?j=eyJ1IjoiNndtMGMifQ.FKZnV4yDO9r1W3mXiFPvoTkXx7p4iMXPKOi9UqQpNhQ)

An AMA moderated by me is included at the end.

Contrast them, thoughts welcome.

# 🍐#143 Closing chapters, acquisitions, and sabbaticals. 

Hey,

Big things happened to your favorite markepear🍐. And because of that I’ve decided to go on a sabbatical for a few months. I’ll still write this newsletter and blog during the break but I am just not sure how frequently.

Took me a while to write this. Needed a minute to put what I feel in words. But the **[neptune.ai](https://link.mail.beehiiv.com/v1/c/AiOKXOZcstHcsk9M8H6qKQXzU0WTPjUxD3jWmTzrKVyrqQ3yCFZZ%2BW197n4B%0AO8sxg%2BC07sH4WqlRMpVgxDGytAj3VPNfeonGGUNAfmeAe6hyd1TvhfqAq%2Bd1%0APyHLSfbGonuKuGDgBPia3aUaxE9TSss2iT4p309KucqvhL0lY6j4zsj%2FOrM8%0A4BWfMWIKjkQV%0A/bb5b4d1e1b808b1a)** **chapter of my career is really officially over**. Happy, proud, nostalgic, sad. Tired (though this one could be because of our new 2month old addition to the family;)).

In December we’ve been [acquired by OpenAI](https://link.mail.beehiiv.com/v1/c/0e8%2B4%2Br%2FjhsZV%2B9XFTFqCl1JdUvY7RY8WJ2NsN5QbUuVkjm2GKV%2FBUMS%2BCUy%0ATLjDLeDBuammL%2FosX34thZpNAdIEBSKo%2FrtbWVGcmXoEYCm91DrCDXEXJXCS%0AtIZinKydk39As2armX%2BVC1OY9HeL7HLs1Hlgk45RwMBjjrSPs0Zk%2F5RPOQd6%0ASP15N9SZ%2Bbp7%0A/8ea4d8de2078ae4f) and a moonshot goal that I put on one of our internal presentations, that “the training run that gets us to AGI will be logged to Neptune” may actually turn out to be true. Time will tell.

And **Neptune is winding down it’s operations completely** (so you may want to screenshot some of those cool things we’ve done on the website if you haven’t already ;)).

**Thanks to Neptune I found my true passion** -> developer marketing. I was a chess pro, poker player, theoretical physicist, stock trader, and a data scientist. And yet marketing to devs gave me so much joy that I’ve decided to create [Developer Markepear](https://link.mail.beehiiv.com/v1/c/alEkPXCmMyJEQiAEgIid%2BInOEFk%2BEXjX53xHoRBfccPOjPZSY%2F2%2BhdonDFWX%0A6c%2Bdccy9jfz5SFmZFtDDk8uFXl04ci9C%2FOyIdGINTbG8Hs9fQ4LnmibV4Pi1%0AY7SzUuqUEZjWmngIZ7g4PR686TPVJyoWIpEydF%2BYj5SO3CjoPEY8y2XDafKy%0AXr%2F6wqp17fAn%0A/0c906fc073bf45f9) and to share my learnings with others.

Extremely happy that cards aligned this way and a moment of “somebody needs to learn marketing” hit us at Neptune. And with my love for learning messy things I decided to take a leap.

**Huge thank you** to:

* all the amazing people who worked on our **marketing/GTM** **team** (do let me know **if you are hiring, some folks are still exploring**),
* **advisors** who helped me learn along the way,
* **leadership and founders** as we worked through thick and thin,
* **investors** for their wisdom and poise when we thought we were smart (and probably were just smartasses),
* and **all the amazing neptune people** I met along the way that made this journey so much more fun.
* my business partner **Piotr, CEO**, the driver of change who pushed me to where I’d never push myself. I wouldn't be where I am now if it wasn’t for him.
* and finally **my wife Magda** (I know you are reading this for the pear puns but still ;)) for supporting me throughout this whole time. You are my rock. Thank you.

And while many Neptuners went to OpenAI and other exciting places **I am taking a sabbatical**. Neptune's acquisition coincided with my second kiddo being born. And while in startups there never seems to be a good time to take rest, it is hard to find a better spot than this.

So for the next few months the only role that I have lined up is CDO (Chief Dad Officer). And after that back to marketing cool stuff ;)

# new blog post: ​moving away from Tailwind, and learning to structure my CSS​

one post this week:

## [Moving away from Tailwind, and learning to structure my CSS](https://60787c41.click.convertkit-mail4.com/qdue872z9eh7h45mdn2clh8gexpvgu4hw2lv/owhkhqhwvn6xrobv/aHR0cHM6Ly9qdm5zLmNhL2Jsb2cvMjAyNi8wNS8xNS9tb3ZpbmctYXdheS1mcm9tLXRhaWx3aW5kLS1hbmQtbGVhcm5pbmctdG8tc3RydWN0dXJlLW15LWNzcy0v)

Hello! 8 years ago, I [wrote excitedly about discovering Tailwind](https://60787c41.click.convertkit-mail4.com/qdue872z9eh7h45mdn2clh8gexpvgu4hw2lv/z2hghnhev7k530sp/aHR0cHM6Ly9qdm5zLmNhL2Jsb2cvMjAxOC8xMS8wMS90YWlsd2luZC0td3JpdGUtY3NzLXdpdGhvdXQtdGhlLWNzcy8=).

At that time I really had no idea how to structure my CSS code and given the
choice between a pile of complete chaos and Tailwind, I was really happy to choose
Tailwind. It helped me make a lot of tiny sites!

I spent the last week or so migrating a couple of sites away from Tailwind and
towards more semantic HTML + vanilla CSS, and it was SO fun and SO interesting,
so here are some things I learned!

As usual I’m not a full-time frontend developer and so all of my CSS learning
has happened in fits and starts over many years.

### it turns out Tailwind taught me a lot

When I started thinking about structuring CSS, I was intimidated at first: I’m
not very good at structuring my CSS! But then I started reading blog posts
talking about how to structure CSS (like [A whole cascade of layers](https://60787c41.click.convertkit-mail4.com/qdue872z9eh7h45mdn2clh8gexpvgu4hw2lv/p8heh9h40d2rzriq/aHR0cHM6Ly93d3cubWlyaWFtc3V6YW5uZS5jb20vMjAyMi8wOS8wNi9sYXllcnMv) or [How I write CSS in 2024](https://60787c41.click.convertkit-mail4.com/qdue872z9eh7h45mdn2clh8gexpvgu4hw2lv/x0hph6he6zpkwob5/aHR0cHM6Ly9qYWNvYmIubnljL3dyaXRpbmcvaG93LWktd3JpdGUtY3NzLWluLTIwMjQ=))
and I realized a couple of things:

1. Every CSS code base has a bunch of different things going on (layouts! fonts! colours! common components!)
2. It’s extremely useful to have systems or guidelines to manage each of those things, otherwise things descend into chaos
3. Tailwind has systems for some of these, and I already know those systems! Maybe I can imitate the systems I like!

For example, Tailwind has:

- a reset stylesheet
- a [colour palette](https://60787c41.click.convertkit-mail4.com/qdue872z9eh7h45mdn2clh8gexpvgu4hw2lv/6qheh8hlgw5x7rfo/aHR0cHM6Ly9qdm5zLmNhL2Jsb2cvMjAyNi8wNS8wNC9jc3MtY29sb3VyLXBhbGV0dGVzLw==)
- a [font scale](https://60787c41.click.convertkit-mail4.com/qdue872z9eh7h45mdn2clh8gexpvgu4hw2lv/kkhmh6hnqe5zlvul/aHR0cHM6Ly92Mi50YWlsd2luZGNzcy5jb20vZG9jcy9mb250LXNpemU=)

### the systems I’m going to talk about

I’m going to talk about a few aspects of my CSS codebase and my thoughts so far
what kind of rules I want to impose on the codebase for each one. Some of them
are copied from Tailwind and some aren’t.

1. reset
2. components
3. colours
4. font sizes
5. utility classes
6. the base
7. spacing
8. responsive design
9. the build system

### 1. reset

I just copied Tailwind’s “[preflight styles](https://60787c41.click.convertkit-mail4.com/qdue872z9eh7h45mdn2clh8gexpvgu4hw2lv/58hvh7hg80n3m8s6/aHR0cHM6Ly92Mi50YWlsd2luZGNzcy5jb20vZG9jcy9wcmVmbGlnaHQ=)”
by going into `tailwind.css` and copying the first 200 lines or so.

I noticed that I’ve developed a relationship with Tailwind’s CSS reset over time,
for example Tailwind sets `box-sizing: border-box` on every element (which means
that an element’s width includes its padding):

```
* { box-sizing: border-box; }

```
I think it would be a real adjustment for me to switch to writing CSS without
these, and I’m sure there are lots of other things in the Tailwind reset (like `html {line-height: 1.5;}`) that I’m subconsciously used to and don’t even realize are
there.
